question:
In 1885 the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus published the results of a curious experiment conducted on a single subject: himself. Memorising lists of meaningless syllables such as 'wid' and 'zof', he tested how many he could recall after intervals ranging from twenty minutes to a month. The results, plotted as a graph, produced what is now called the forgetting curve: memory falls steeply in the first hours after learning and then declines more gradually. Without review, most of what is learned is lost within days. He repeated the exercise many times with fresh lists, so that chance and fatigue would not distort the pattern, and the shape of the curve proved remarkably consistent.

For more than a century, the curve was read as a lament about the frailty of the mind, and students were urged to cram, repeat and revise ever harder. Recent researchers, however, caution that forgetting is not merely a failure. A memory that retained every detail would be clogged with trivia and unable to pick out what matters; the capacity to let go of outdated information, such as last year's telephone number, is what allows the mind to generalise and adapt. On this view, forgetting is a feature of a healthy memory, and the real puzzle is not why we forget but why we remember anything at all.

The curve does, nonetheless, carry a practical lesson. Ebbinghaus found that each act of review slowed the decay, so that material revisited at widening intervals, after a day, then a week, then a month, could be retained far longer than material studied once, however intensely. This 'spaced repetition' has since been confirmed in many studies and is now built into language-learning software. It is worth remembering, though, that Ebbinghaus tested nonsense syllables. The meaningful material that students actually study, rich in connections to what they already know, is forgotten more slowly, and the slope of the curve in everyday learning is gentler than his original graph suggests.

Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: The forgetting curve, once read as a sign of mental weakness, is now seen as reflecting a useful feature of memory, and it also offers practical lessons for study.
Ebbinghaus's experiments on nonsense syllables have been shown to be worthless for understanding everyday learning.
Cramming is the most effective way of defeating the forgetting curve.
A memory that retains every detail would be ideal for learners.

explanation:
नियम: Main idea / central idea वही विकल्प है जो पूरे passage का सार समेटे। गलत विकल्प प्रायः चार प्रकार के होते हैं: (i) Too narrow — केवल एक paragraph या एक detail की बात; (ii) Out of scope — passage में है ही नहीं; (iii) Extreme / distorted — always, never, only, sole, completely जैसे चरम शब्द या बात को तोड़-मरोड़कर पेश करना; (iv) Opposite — लेखक के मत के उलट।

यहाँ: सही उत्तर (A)। Para 1: Ebbinghaus का experiment और curve। Para 2: curve को कमज़ोरी मानने की पुरानी सोच के बजाय भूलना स्मृति की उपयोगी विशेषता है। Para 3: curve से व्यावहारिक सीख (spaced repetition)। यही विकल्प तीनों हिस्सों को जोड़ता है।

अन्य विकल्प:
(B) — Extreme: passage केवल इतना कहता है कि सार्थक सामग्री धीमे भूली जाती है और वास्तविक curve कम तीखा है; प्रयोग को 'worthless' नहीं बताता।

(D) — Opposite: Para 2 में कहा गया कि हर बात याद रखने वाली स्मृति फ़ालतू बातों से भर जाती और ज़रूरी चीज़ें नहीं चुन पाती।

question:
For almost the whole of human history, the night sky was the common inheritance of every person on Earth. Navigators steered by it, farmers read their seasons from it, and every culture wove myths around its patterns. Today, a child born in a large city may never see the Milky Way. Artificial light, spilling upwards and scattering in the atmosphere, produces a luminous haze called skyglow, and astronomers estimate that a large share of humanity now lives beneath skies too bright for the galaxy to be seen. Even the countryside is not spared, since the glow of a distant city can wash out faint stars many kilometres away.

Light pollution is usually dismissed as a matter of aesthetics, a loss of beauty that must be accepted as the price of safety and progress. The evidence suggests the cost is greater. Many creatures have evolved to depend on darkness: sea-turtle hatchlings, which find the sea by the brightness of the horizon, wander inland towards streetlights; migrating birds, disoriented by lit towers, collide with buildings in their thousands; and nocturnal insects, drawn to lamps, circle until they die of exhaustion. In humans, exposure to bright light at night suppresses the hormone melatonin and disrupts the body clock, and researchers have begun to investigate links with sleep disorders and other illnesses, although the findings are still preliminary.

The remedy, unusually for an environmental problem, is cheap and well understood. Shielding lamps so that they direct light downwards, using warmer colours and dimmer bulbs, and switching lights off when they are not needed can reduce glare without compromising safety. Several towns and parks have been designated 'dark-sky' places, and some have found that tourism has grown as a result. The obstacle is not technology but habit: a culture that equates brightness with security finds it hard to believe that less light might sometimes be better. Restoring the night, it seems, is a matter of will rather than invention.

Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: Myths of the Ancient Night Sky
Losing the Night: The Hidden Costs and Simple Cures of Light Pollution
How Streetlights Make Our Cities Safer
The Plight of Sea Turtles and Migrating Birds

explanation:
नियम: Title वह होना चाहिए जो पूरे passage को समेटे और संक्षिप्त हो। बहुत narrow (केवल एक हिस्सा), out of scope (passage से बाहर) या लेखक के मत के उलट वाला title गलत होता है।

यहाँ: सही उत्तर (B)। Passage की रूपरेखा: Para 1 में रात के आसमान का खोना, Para 2 में छिपी हानियाँ (जीव-जंतु और मानव), Para 3 में सस्ता और सरल उपाय। 'Hidden Costs and Simple Cures' इन सबको समेटता है।

अन्य विकल्प:
(A) Myths of the Ancient Night Sky — Too narrow: प्राचीन आकाश और मिथकों का ज़िक्र केवल Para 1 की भूमिका है, passage का विषय नहीं।
(C) — Opposite: लेखक रोशनी को सुरक्षा के नाम पर होने वाले नुकसान के रूप में देखता है और कम, सही दिशा वाली रोशनी की वकालत करता है।
(D) — Too narrow: कछुए और पक्षी केवल प्रभावों के उदाहरण हैं; passage का केंद्र पूरी समस्या और उसका समाधान है।

Navigators steered by it, farmers read their seasons from it, and every culture wove myths around its patterns. Today, a child born in a large city may never see the Milky Way. Artificial light, spilling upwards and scattering in the atmosphere, produces a luminous haze called skyglow, and astronomers estimate that a large share of humanity now lives beneath skies too bright for the galaxy to be seen. Even the countryside is not spared, since the glow of a distant city can wash out faint stars many kilometres away.

Light pollution is usually dismissed as a matter of aesthetics, a loss of beauty that must be accepted as the price of safety and progress. The evidence suggests the cost is greater. Many creatures have evolved to depend on darkness: sea-turtle hatchlings, which find the sea by the brightness of the horizon, wander inland towards streetlights; migrating birds, disoriented by lit towers, collide with buildings in their thousands; and nocturnal insects, drawn to lamps, circle until they die of exhaustion. In humans, exposure to bright light at night suppresses the hormone melatonin and disrupts the body clock, and researchers have begun to investigate links with sleep disorders and other illnesses, although the findings are still preliminary.

The remedy, unusually for an environmental problem, is cheap and well understood. Shielding lamps so that they direct light downwards, using warmer colours and dimmer bulbs, and switching lights off when they are not needed can reduce glare without compromising safety. Several towns and parks have been designated 'dark-sky' places, and some have found that tourism has grown as a result. The obstacle is not technology but habit: a culture that equates brightness with security finds it hard to believe that less light might sometimes be better. Restoring the night, it seems, is a matter of will rather than invention.

question:
Few debates in the museum world are as heated as the question of whether objects taken from their places of origin should be returned. The great museums of Europe and North America hold vast collections assembled during the age of empire, when treasures were bought, gifted, exchanged or simply seized. The countries that lost these objects regard them as stolen fragments of their heritage, and a growing number are demanding their return. In recent years some institutions have agreed: bronzes looted from the kingdom of Benin, for example, have been handed back to Nigeria by museums and universities in several countries.

Museums that resist return advance arguments that deserve a hearing, even if not all of them persuade. They say that objects in a universal museum can be seen by millions of visitors from every nation, encouraging a sense of shared human history; that they have been conserved with resources that source countries may lack; and that opening the door to restitution would empty the great collections, since almost every object has a contested past. Some of these claims are weaker than they appear. Conservation capacity is not fixed and is improving in many places, and the argument that visitors benefit from seeing objects abroad would justify, by the same logic, the removal of any treasure to any wealthy country.

Between the extremes, a middle path is emerging. Long-term loans, shared custody and travelling exhibitions allow objects to circulate without settling the question of ownership, while joint research and training help source countries build their own capacity. Such arrangements are unlikely to satisfy those who regard return as a matter of justice rather than convenience. But they reflect a recognition that the question is not whether the past was unjust, which few would deny, but how the present should respond. A museum's duty, on this view, is not merely to keep what it holds but to give a truthful account of how it came to hold it.

Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?

options.text: Museums should immediately return every object acquired during the age of empire.
Source countries lack the resources to conserve their own heritage.
Universal museums have lost their purpose and should be closed.

explanation:
नियम: Main idea / central idea वही विकल्प है जो पूरे passage का सार समेटे। गलत विकल्प प्रायः चार प्रकार के होते हैं: (i) Too narrow — केवल एक paragraph या एक detail की बात; (ii) Out of scope — passage में है ही नहीं; (iii) Extreme / distorted — always, never, only, sole, completely जैसे चरम शब्द या बात को तोड़-मरोड़कर पेश करना; (iv) Opposite — लेखक के मत के उलट।

The washing machine that lasted two decades in a grandmother's kitchen has a modern successor that, by many accounts, is built to survive barely half as long. Consumers have long suspected that products are designed to fail, and the suspicion has a name: planned obsolescence. Economists point out, however, that the matter is more complicated than a conspiracy. Manufacturers face genuine pressures to cut costs and weight, and consumers themselves often prefer a cheaper product with newer features to a durable one that looks dated within a few years.

question:
In 1906 the statistician Francis Galton attended a country fair where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed. Nearly eight hundred people entered, most of them with no expertise in livestock. Galton, who was inclined to distrust the judgement of the masses, collected the tickets, expecting to demonstrate their folly. To his surprise, the average of the guesses came within a few pounds of the true weight, more accurately than the great majority of the individual guesses. The 'wisdom of the crowd' had been, in a manner of speaking, discovered by a sceptic.

The result is often cited as proof that crowds are wise, but this conclusion is too sweeping. A crowd is wise only under particular conditions. Its members must hold diverse perspectives, so that their errors point in different directions and cancel out; they must form their judgements independently, rather than copying one another; and there must be some way of combining their opinions into a single estimate. When these conditions fail, the effect can be reversed. Had the visitors at Galton's fair shouted their guesses aloud, the early estimates would have influenced later ones, and a collective mistake might have been magnified instead of corrected. Financial bubbles, in which investors follow the herd into overpriced assets, show how a crowd that watches itself can be spectacularly foolish.

The lesson has practical consequences for those who design organisations. Committees in which junior members wait to hear the chairperson's view before speaking destroy independence, and so do meetings in which the loudest voice sets the agenda. Some firms now ask participants to write down their estimates privately before discussion begins, and to combine them afterwards. The method sounds simple, even trivial, but it rests on a real insight: the wisdom of a group lies not in the group as such but in the way its members' separate judgements are gathered. A crowd, in short, is wise only when each of its members is allowed to think independently, and sometimes uncomfortably, for himself or herself.

question:
In 1906 the statistician Francis Galton attended a country fair where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed. Nearly eight hundred people entered, most of them with no expertise in livestock. Galton, who was inclined to distrust the judgement of the masses, collected the tickets, expecting to demonstrate their folly. To his surprise, the average of the guesses came within a few pounds of the true weight, more accurately than the great majority of the individual guesses. The 'wisdom of the crowd' had been, in a manner of speaking, discovered by a sceptic.

The result is often cited as proof that crowds are wise, but this conclusion is too sweeping. A crowd is wise only under particular conditions. Its members must hold diverse perspectives, so that their errors point in different directions and cancel out; they must form their judgements independently, rather than copying one another; and there must be some way of combining their opinions into a single estimate. When these conditions fail, the effect can be reversed. Had the visitors at Galton's fair shouted their guesses aloud, the early estimates would have influenced later ones, and a collective mistake might have been magnified instead of corrected. Financial bubbles, in which investors follow the herd into overpriced assets, show how a crowd that watches itself can be spectacularly foolish.

The lesson has practical consequences for those who design organisations. Committees in which junior members wait to hear the chairperson's view before speaking destroy independence, and so do meetings in which the loudest voice sets the agenda. Some firms now ask participants to write down their estimates privately before discussion begins, and to combine them afterwards. The method sounds simple, even trivial, but it rests on a real insight: the wisdom of a group lies not in the group as such but in the way its members' separate judgements are gathered. A crowd, in short, is wise only when each of its members is allowed to think independently, and sometimes uncomfortably, for himself or herself.
